GraSP-STL: A Graph-Based Framework for Zero-Shot Signal Temporal
Logic Planning via Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
Ancheng Hou, Ruijia Liu and Xiang Yin
Abstract— This paper studies offline, zero-shot planning un-
der Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications. We assume
access only to an offline dataset of state-action-state transi-
tions collected by a task-agnostic behavior policy, with no
analytical dynamics model, no further environment interaction,
and no task-specific retraining. The objective is to synthe-
size a control strategy whose resulting trajectory satisfies an
arbitrary unseen STL specification. To this end, we propose
GraSP-STL, a graph-search-based framework for zero-shot
STL planning from offline trajectories. The method learns a
goal-conditioned value function from offline data and uses it
to induce a finite-horizon reachability metric over the state
space. Based on this metric, it constructs a directed graph
abstraction whose nodes represent representative states and
whose edges encode feasible short-horizon transitions. Planning
is then formulated as a graph search over waypoint sequences,
evaluated using arithmetic-geometric mean robustness and its
interval semantics, and executed by a learned goal-conditioned
policy. The proposed framework separates reusable reachability
learning from task-conditioned planning, enabling zero-shot
generalization to unseen STL tasks and long-horizon planning
through the composition of short-horizon behaviors from offline
data. Experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness on a
range of offline STL planning tasks.
I. INTRODUCTION
Signal Temporal Logic (STL) is a formal language for
specifying complex temporal tasks for dynamical systems
with both temporal and spatial constraints, allowing the
formalization of objectives such as sequencing, timing, and
safety requirements. By leveraging formal reasoning, STL
enables the synthesis of control inputs or plans that guarantee
the satisfaction of these specifications with provable correct-
ness. In recent years, STL has been widely applied across
various engineering domains where precise specification and
reliable execution of temporal behaviors are critical [1], [2].
When an accurate system model is available, optimization-
based methods are a standard approach for STL control syn-
thesis [3], [4]. By encoding specifications as mixed-integer
or nonlinear programs, they systematically handle logical
and temporal constraints. Despite numerous improved vari-
ants [5], [6], these methods often face scalability issues as the
state dimension, planning horizon, or specification complex-
ity increases. Sampling-based methods, such as RRT [7], [8],
partially address this by exploring trajectories and evaluating
STL robustness without explicit state-space discretization,

to construct.
Learning-based methods offer a promising alternative for
STL control synthesis without explicit system models. A
common approach uses reinforcement learning (RL), en-
coding STL objectives into reward functions and optimiz-
ing policies through interaction with the environment [9],
[10], [11]. While effective in some cases, RL depends on
online data, making it unsuitable for purely offline settings,
and learned policies are typically task-specific, limiting
generalization. Long-horizon STL tasks remain challenging
due to sparse and delayed rewards. End-to-end learning
pipelines [12], [13] can address offline scenarios by mapping
observations directly to behaviors, but they often require
substantial expert data and generalize poorly to unseen
specifications.
Recently, hierarchical planning frameworks [14] have
aimed to improve task generalization by integrating logic-
level planning with learned models of system dynamics.
By decomposing STL formulas into intermediate temporal
subgoals and solving them with reusable learned modules,
these methods achieve zero-shot generalization to unseen
tasks without task-specific retraining. Nonetheless, they often
entail high computational costs and require sufficiently rich
data to support subgoal transitions, making them less prac-
tical when only fragmented offline trajectories are available.
In this work, we focus on a model-free offline setting for
STL planning, where no analytical system model or online
environment interaction is available. Instead, we assume
access only to a collection of offline system trajectories, po-
tentially fragmented and collected via arbitrary task-agnostic
policies. This setting presents two primary challenges. First,
the planner must rely entirely on offline data, without query-
ing the environment or refining decisions through online
interaction. Second, long-horizon STL tasks are particularly
difficult, as individual trajectory fragments are often short
and may not directly satisfy the target specification. Address-
ing unseen STL tasks in a zero-shot manner thus requires
inferring a reusable finite-horizon reachability structure from
offline data to stitch short-horizon behaviors into coherent
long-horizon plans.
To address these challenges, we proposeGraSP-STL, a
graph-search-based framework for zero-shot STL planning
from offline trajectories. It learns a goal-conditioned value
function to induce a finite-horizon reachability measure and
constructs a directed graph where nodes represent represen-
tative states and edges encode feasible short-horizon transi-arXiv:2603.29533v1  [cs.RO]  31 Mar 2026

tions. Planning a given STL specification is formulated as
a graph-search problem over candidate waypoint sequences,
with partial and complete plans evaluated using arithmetic-
geometric mean (AGM) robustness [15], [8]. This enables
long-horizon plans to be synthesized by stitching together
short-horizon transitions from offline data, executed via a
goal-conditioned policy. Our contributions are: (i) formaliz-
ing purely offline zero-shot STL planning with only frag-
mented task-agnostic trajectories, (ii) developing a graph-
based reachability abstraction for long-horizon planning, (iii)
integrating AGM robustness into graph search for structured
STL planning, and (iv) demonstrating effective and inter-
pretable solutions to unseen long-horizon STL tasks.
II. PRELIMINARIES

B. Signal Temporal Logic
We adopt signal temporal logic (STL) specification [16] to
describe formal temporal properties defined over the sampled
real-valued signals. The syntax of STL formulaeϕis:
ϕ:=⊤ |µ| ¬ϕ|ϕ 1∧ϕ2|ϕ1∨ϕ2|G[a,b]ϕ1|F[a,b]ϕ1,(3)
where⊤is the true predicate,µis an atomic predicate
associated with an evaluation functionh µ:Rn→R,
i.e., predicateµis satisfied at statexiffh µ(x)≥0. The
boolean operators¬,∧, and∨denote negation, conjunction,
and disjunction, respectively. Thetemporal operatorsG [a,b]
andF [a,b] denote “always” and “eventually” over the time
interval[a, b], wherea, b∈Z ≥0anda≤b.The boolean satisfaction of a given signalsat timetwith
respect to an STL formulaϕis denoted ass t|=ϕ, and we

semantics can be found in [16].
C. AGM Robustness and Interval Semantics
In addition to boolean satisfaction, STL also admits a
quantitative semantics known as robustness, which measures
the degree to which a signal satisfies or violates an STL
formula. The original robustness [17] of a signalsis
defined over min-max operations, which can lead to non-
smoothness and sensitivity to local extrema. In this work,
we adopt the arithmetic-geometric mean (AGM) robustness
semantics for STL from [15], which provides a smoother and
more informative measure of satisfaction by replacing min-
max with differentiable approximations. This property makes
it particularly suitable for evaluating candidate trajectories
during graph search.
For a complete signalsand an STL formulaϕ, let
ηs,ϕ(t)∈[−1,1]denote the AGM robustness ofϕat timet,
where positive and negative values indicate satisfaction and
violation, respectively. For predicate formulas, the evaluation
functionh µis normalized to ehµ∈[−1,1], ensuring that the
resulting robustness values remain within this range. When
the signal is clear from context, we writeη ϕ(t)for brevity.
When only a partial signal is available, we adopt the interval
semantics in [8]. Specifically,
[η]ϕ(t):= [ηϕ(t),ηϕ(t)]⊆[−1,1],(4)
denotes the range of AGM robustness values over all com-
pletions of the current partial signal. This interval semantics
is sound, in the sense that it bounds the robustness of every
completion, and it converges to the exact robustness once the
observed signal length reaches the STL horizon∥ϕ∥[8].
For temporal operators, the interval semantics in [8] eval-
uates the observed portion of the temporal window using the
standard AGM rule, and obtains the lower and upper bounds
by replacing each unobserved value with its worst-case
and best-case completion, namely−1and1, respectively.
When the child subformula has no temporal dependence
of its own, this aggregation can be updated incrementally
using the modification rules in [8], which yields an efficient
monitor for non-nested STL formulae. Our method keeps
this interval-monitoring framework and extends it to arbitrary
nested temporal operators.
III. PROBLEMFORMULATION
In this work, we study the problem of zero-shot, model-
free STL planning. Specifically, we assume access to an
offline dataset
D= (x t,at,xt+1),(5)
which is collected by a task-agnostic behavior policy. This
dataset is used solely for representation learning, and no
further interaction with the environment or task-specific
retraining is permitted.
Given an initial statex 0and an STL specificationϕ
defined over the signals, the objective is to synthesize a

control strategy such that the resulting trajectory satisfiesϕ.
In our framework, this objective is achieved by generating
a high-level waypoint plan, which is subsequently executed
by a learned goal-conditioned policy.
IV. OVERALLFRAMEWORK
Figure 1 illustrates the overall GraSP-STL pipeline. The
framework consists of three main components:
(i) anoffline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning
(GCRL) agentthat provides a reachability measure
(represented by a value function) and a corresponding
execution policy;
(ii) agraph constructionmodule that builds a directed
graph whose nodes are representative states and whose
edges encode feasiblek-step transitions under the
learned measure; and
(iii) agraph-searchmodule that finds an STL-satisfying
graph node sequence using AGM robustness intervals to
evaluate partial plans. The resulting waypoint sequence
is then executed by the learned policy.
Following common terminology in hierarchical plan-
ning, we refer to the graph node sequence gener-
ated by graph search aswaypoints, denoted byw=
(w0,w1,w2,w3, . . . ,w N), wherew iis the selected graph
node at time stepi. In the ideal case, the sampled signal
induced by executing the low-level controller coincides with
the planned waypoint sequence, i.e.,s=w, so STL satisfac-
tion can be evaluated directly onw. In practice, execution er-
rors and approximation errors may cause deviations, i.e.,s̸=
w. Nevertheless, as the goal-conditioned policy is trained
to realize short-horizon transitions between waypoints, the
executed signal is expected to remain sufficiently close to
the planned sequence, thereby ensuring that waypoint-level
STL evaluation remains informative.
V. GOAL-CONDITIONEDREACHABILITYMEASURE AND
POLICYLEARNING

offline datasetDa goal-conditioned value function and a
goal-conditioned policy. The former induces a reachability
measure for planning, while the latter tracks target states
with estimated transition steps within the pre-defined finite
horizon. Since the graph abstraction is built from the learned
measure and later executed by this policy, these two compo-
nents must operate on the same transition scale.

VI. GRAPHCONSTRUCTION
Given the learned transition measure, we construct a
directed graphG= (V,E), where nodes correspond to
representative states and edges encode feasible transitions
within a control horizonk.
Node Construction.We first construct graph nodes via
a two-stage sampling and clustering procedure. Instead of
directly using the full dataset, we perform a geometric grid-
based uniform subsampling over the state space to improve
spatial coverage. Specifically, observations are partitioned
into grid cells, and a fixed number of samples are drawn
approximately uniformly across occupied cells.
On the sampled observations, we perform temporal-
distance-aware clustering as in [19]. Given a set of candidate
states, we compute pairwise learned distances and group
states whose distances fall below a threshold proportional
to the horizonk. Each cluster is represented by its medoid,
namely, the state minimizing the total intra-cluster distance.
The resulting set of representative nodesVprovides a
compact abstraction that preserves both geometric coverage
and consistency under the learned distance metric.
Edge Construction.For each pair of nodesv i,vj∈ V,
we compute the learned transition distance ˆd(vi,vj). Self-
transitions are excluded by setting ˆd(vi,vi) =∞. An edge
fromv itovjis considered feasible if
ˆd(vi,vj)< k−δ,(11)
whereδis a safety margin considering estimation errors and
execution uncertainties. This defines a candidate neighbor set
for each node.
To construct a sparse yet well-structured graph, we select
neighbors using a directional diversity strategy. Specifically,
the 2D space around each node is partitioned into angular
bins, and at most one neighbor is selected per bin. Within
each bin, candidates are ranked by adistance efficiencyscore
∥vj−vi∥2
ˆd(vi,vj),(12)
which favors transitions that achieve larger geometric
progress per unit learned distance.
If the number of selected neighbors is below a target
degree, additional neighbors are iteratively added by pri-
oritizing (i) angular novelty relative to already selected
edges and (ii) distance efficiency. Furthermore, edges are
made approximately bidirectional: wheneverv i→v jis
selected and the reverse transition also satisfies the feasibility
condition, the reverse edgev j→v iis added.
Graph Refinement.The resulting graph may not be fully
strongly connected. To ensure global reachability for plan-
ning, we extract the largest strongly connected component
(SCC) and discard all other nodes and edges. The final graph
G= (V,E)is defined on this largest SCC.VII. GRAPHSEARCH FORSTL PLANNING
Given the constructed graphG= (V,E), we formulate the
high-levelSTL planning problem as a graph search over an
augmented state space that jointly captures system evolution
and STL satisfaction. Given a start statex 0and an STL
specificationϕ, we search for a waypoint sequencew=
(w0,w1,w2,w3, . . . ,w N)whose execution by the learned
goal-conditioned policy is expected to satisfyϕ. We do not
requirex 0∈ V, since the initial state need not coincide with
a graph node.
A. STL Robustness Evaluation
The main challenge in waypoint-based STL planning is
to evaluate the robustness interval of apartialwaypoint

The key distinction is whether the child of a temporal
operator can change retroactively as new states are appended.
This does not occur for non-temporal subformulae, but it
does for nested temporal ones. For instance, ifχ=F [0,2]µ,

updated by a constant-time append rule alone.
We therefore call a subformulaψimmutableif its robust-

VIII. EXPERIMENTS
A. Experimental Setup
Environments and Datasets.We evaluate the proposed
GraSP-STL framework on theANTMAZEenvironment of

C. Large-Scale Evaluation
For the large-scale evaluation, we perform the proposed
graph-based STL planning procedure on 2400 tasks gen-

procedure and the robustness of the learned reachability

failure modes emerge across task types. For sequential tasks
with tight temporal constraints (e.g., T6), planning suc-
cess remains high while execution degrades, suggesting that
temporally tight schedules leave limited slack and increase
sensitivity to tracking errors. In contrast, for persistence tasks
with consecutive global constraints (e.g., T9), both planning
and execution success rates are lower. This is becauseG
operators require the agent to enter a region at the start
of the time window and remain until its end, significantly
compressing the available transition time between regions.
As a result, both planning feasibility and execution tolerance
are reduced.
IX. CONCLUSION
We proposed GraSP-STL, a graph-based framework for
zero-shot STL planning without explicit system dynamics
or task-specific retraining. By learning a transition mea-
sure from offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning,
the framework constructs a graph abstraction and performs
STL planning via graph search with incremental robust-
ness evaluation. Experimental results demonstrated strong
performance on diverse long-horizon STL tasks with good
computational efficiency. Despite these promising results, the
current framework still depends on offline data coverage,
relies on a discrete graph abstraction, and may produce
temporally tight plans with limited execution slack. Future
work will investigate slack-aware planning, adaptive graphrefinement, and extensions to safety-critical and uncertainty-
aware execution.

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This document introduces GraSP-STL, a novel graph-search-based framework for zero-shot Signal Temporal Logic (STL) planning using offline data. The core problem addressed is planning for arbitrary, unseen STL specifications from a dataset of state-action-state transitions collected by a task-agnostic policy, without access to an analytical dynamics model or the ability to interact with the environment further.

The main points covered are:

*   **Problem Setting:** The paper focuses on a model-free, offline setting for STL planning, where only fragmented, task-agnostic trajectories are available. This presents challenges in long-horizon planning and generalization to unseen specifications.
*   **GraSP-STL Framework:** The proposed framework learns a goal-conditioned value function from offline data to estimate reachability. This metric is used to construct a directed graph where nodes represent states and edges represent feasible short-horizon transitions.
*   **Planning as Graph Search:** Planning for an STL specification is then formulated as a graph search over waypoint sequences. This search is guided by a measure of robustness, specifically using Arithmetic-Geometric Mean (AGM) robustness and its interval semantics.
*   **Zero-Shot Generalization:** The framework aims to achieve zero-shot generalization to unseen STL tasks by separating reusable reachability learning from task-conditioned planning. Long-horizon plans are synthesized by composing short-horizon behaviors extracted from the offline data.
*   **Key Contributions:** The paper highlights its contributions in formalizing offline zero-shot STL planning, developing a graph-based reachability abstraction, integrating AGM robustness into graph search, and demonstrating effective and interpretable solutions for unseen long-horizon STL tasks.
*   **Preliminaries:** The document also provides background on the system model (discrete-time control systems with unknown dynamics), Signal Temporal Logic (STL) syntax and semantics, and the concept of AGM robustness and interval semantics for quantitative evaluation of STL specifications.

structure.title: PROBLEM FORMULATION
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a framework called GraSP-STL for planning and executing trajectories that satisfy Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications. The core idea is to formulate STL planning as a graph-search problem over candidate waypoint sequences. Key aspects covered include:

*   **Problem Formulation:** Planning is framed as a graph-search problem using candidate waypoint sequences, with plans evaluated using Arithmetic-Geometric Mean (AGM) robustness. This allows for long-horizon planning by stitching together short-horizon transitions learned from offline data.
*   **Contributions:** The authors highlight four main contributions:
    *   Formalizing zero-shot, offline STL planning with fragmented, task-agnostic trajectories.
    *   Developing a graph-based reachability abstraction for long-horizon planning.
    *   Integrating AGM robustness into graph search for structured STL planning.
    *   Demonstrating effective and interpretable solutions for unseen long-horizon STL tasks.
*   **Preliminaries:**
    *   **System Model:** Describes a discrete-time control system with unknown dynamics and how system trajectories are subsampled to create a lower-frequency signal for STL evaluation.
    *   **Signal Temporal Logic (STL):** Defines the syntax and semantics of STL, including atomic predicates, boolean operators, and temporal operators (Always "G" and Eventually "F") over time intervals.
    *   **AGM Robustness and Interval Semantics:** Explains the use of AGM robustness as a quantitative measure of STL satisfaction, which is smoother than traditional min-max robustness. It also introduces interval semantics for handling partial signals, bounding the robustness of all possible completions.
*   **Problem Formulation (Detailed):** The problem is defined as zero-shot, model-free STL planning, assuming access to an offline dataset of state-action-next state transitions collected by a task-agnostic policy. The goal is to synthesize a control strategy that results in an STL-satisfying trajectory, achieved by generating a high-level waypoint plan executed by a learned goal-conditioned policy.
*   **Overall Framework (GraSP-STL):** The framework comprises three main components:
    *   An offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (GCRL) agent that provides a reachability measure (value function) and an execution policy.
    *   A graph construction module that builds a directed graph of representative states and feasible transitions.
    *   A graph-search module that finds an STL-satisfying waypoint sequence using AGM robustness intervals.
*   **Goal-Conditioned Reachability Measure and Policy Learning:** This section details the learning of a goal-conditioned value function and policy from the offline dataset.
    *   **Value Function Learning:** The value function is used to estimate transition steps between states, defining a graph construction metric where a higher value indicates greater reachability.
    *   **Policy Learning:** A goal-conditioned policy is trained to execute short-horizon transitions towards target states. The training objective is a weighted behavior cloning approach that incorporates advantage from the value function and a directional similarity term to encourage progress towards the goal.

structure.title: OVERALL FRAMEWORK
structure.summary:
The document describes a framework called GraSP-STL for generating control strategies that satisfy Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications. The core idea is to decompose the problem into a high-level waypoint planning phase and a low-level policy execution phase.

The framework has three main components:
1.  **Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (GCRL) Agent:** This agent learns a value function that estimates reachability (interpreted as transition steps) and a goal-conditioned policy for executing short-horizon transitions towards target states.
2.  **Graph Construction Module:** This module builds a directed graph where nodes represent states and edges represent feasible k-step transitions, guided by the learned reachability measure.
3.  **Graph Search Module:** This module searches the constructed graph for a sequence of nodes (waypoints) that satisfies the STL formula, using AGM robustness intervals to evaluate partial plans.

The generated waypoint sequence is then executed by the learned goal-conditioned policy. The document details how the value function is learned to estimate transition steps (using the negative of the value function) and how the policy is trained using a weighted behavior cloning objective that incorporates advantage and directional similarity terms to encourage progress towards the goal. The goal is to ensure that even with execution errors, the actual trajectory remains close enough to the planned waypoints for the STL satisfaction evaluation to be meaningful.

structure.title: GOAL-CONDITIONED REACHABILITY MEASURE AND POLICY LEARNING
structure.summary:
The document describes the GraSP-STL framework, a method for generating trajectories that satisfy Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications. The framework has three main components:

1.  **Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (GCRL) Agent:** This component learns a value function that estimates reachability (interpreted as transition steps) and a goal-conditioned policy for executing short-horizon transitions towards target states. The value function is used to define a distance metric, and the policy is trained to follow directional control and make effective progress towards goals.

2.  **Graph Construction Module:** This module builds a directed graph where nodes represent representative states. These states are obtained through a two-stage sampling and clustering process that considers the learned transition distances. Edges in the graph represent feasible k-step transitions between these representative states, selected using a directional diversity strategy to ensure sparsity and good coverage. The graph is then refined by extracting the largest strongly connected component to guarantee global reachability.

3.  **Graph Search Module:** This module searches the constructed graph for a sequence of waypoints that, when executed by the learned policy, are expected to satisfy the given STL specification. A key challenge addressed here is the evaluation of STL robustness for partial waypoint sequences during the search. The framework extends an incremental AGM-interval monitor to handle arbitrary nesting of STL operators, recomputing robustness intervals when necessary for non-immutable subformulae.

structure.title: GRAPH CONSTRUCTION
structure.summary:
The document describes a method for constructing a directed graph from learned state transitions and then using this graph for Signal Temporal Logic (STL) planning.

The graph construction involves:
1.  **Node Construction**: Creating representative states by first subsampling the state space using a grid-based approach for coverage, and then applying temporal-distance-aware clustering to group similar states. Each cluster is represented by its medoid.
2.  **Edge Construction**: Defining feasible transitions between nodes based on a learned transition distance and a control horizon. Neighbors are selected using a directional diversity strategy that prioritizes angular novelty and distance efficiency, and edges are made approximately bidirectional.
3.  **Graph Refinement**: Ensuring global reachability for planning by extracting the largest strongly connected component (SCC) of the constructed graph.

Following graph construction, the document details a graph search approach for STL planning:
1.  **Problem Formulation**: The high-level STL planning problem is formulated as a graph search over an augmented state space that considers both system evolution and STL satisfaction. The goal is to find a waypoint sequence expected to satisfy an STL specification.
2.  **STL Robustness Evaluation**: A key challenge addressed is evaluating the robustness interval of a partial waypoint sequence during graph search. This involves extending an incremental interval monitor to handle arbitrarily nested STL formulae.
    *   The concept of "immutable" subformulas is introduced, where robustness is fully determined by the current state.
    *   An update mechanism is described that reuses incremental updates for immutable children of temporal operators and recomputes for non-immutable children, ensuring correctness for nested STL.
    *   The complexity of this evaluation is analyzed, showing it to be efficient for non-nested cases and potentially higher for deeply nested structures.

structure.title: GRAPH SEARCH FOR STL PLANNING
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt details a framework called GraSP-STL for planning with Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications. The main points covered are:

1.  **Graph Construction (VI):**
    *   A directed graph is constructed where nodes represent representative states and edges represent feasible transitions within a control horizon.
    *   **Node Construction:** Involves a two-stage process of uniform subsampling of the state space (grid-based) followed by temporal-distance-aware clustering to identify medoids as representative nodes.
    *   **Edge Construction:** Edges are created based on learned transition distances between nodes, subject to a feasibility condition related to the control horizon and a safety margin. A directional diversity strategy is used to select neighbors, prioritizing distance efficiency and angular novelty. Edges are made approximately bidirectional.
    *   **Graph Refinement:** The largest strongly connected component (SCC) of the graph is extracted to ensure global reachability for planning.

2.  **Graph Search for STL Planning (VII):**
    *   The high-level STL planning problem is formulated as a graph search over an augmented state space that combines graph nodes with the current STL monitor state.
    *   **STL Robustness Evaluation (A):** A key challenge is evaluating the robustness interval of partial waypoint sequences. The document extends an incremental AGM-interval monitor to handle arbitrary nesting of STL formulae. It distinguishes between "immutable" subformulae (whose robustness is determined by current state) and others, adapting update strategies accordingly. The complexity of this evaluation is discussed.
    *   **Graph Search Procedure (B):**
        *   **Search Node:** Defined by the current graph node, predecessor, time step, robustness interval of the full specification, and monitor tables (H, Hraw).
        *   **Initialization:** Uses a virtual start anchor node and initializes the monitor from the initial state.
        *   **Successor Expansion and Pruning:** Nodes are expanded by appending graph states or by a "wait" action. Pruning occurs if the robustness interval becomes non-positive. The search terminates successfully if a satisfying waypoint sequence is found within the time horizon.
        *   **Search Strategy:** Standard frontier policies (BFS, DFS) can be used. The complexity of the search is analyzed, considering branching factor, STL horizon, and evaluation complexity.
        *   **Heuristics:** Heuristics are introduced for frontier prioritization (using a heuristic robustness interval) and dominance-based pruning to improve search efficiency, though these may sacrifice completeness.

3.  **Experiments (VIII):**
    *   **Experimental Setup:** The GraSP-STL framework is evaluated on the ANTMAZE environment from OGBENCH, using an 8-DoF quadruped robot. An offline dataset of trajectories is used for learning and training.
    *   **STL Specifications:** A diverse set of STL specifications from 12 templates are used, categorized by difficulty (Basic, Intermediate, Advanced), covering reachability, sequencing, safety, persistence, branching, and nested operators. Atomic predicates are defined based on spatial regions.
    *   **Case Study:** A representative case study illustrates the framework's application, showing the construction of a reachability graph and its properties.

structure.title: EXPERIMENTS
structure.summary: The partial document discusses methods to improve the efficiency of searching for solutions to Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications. It introduces heuristics for prioritizing search frontiers and dominance-based pruning. Specifically, it defines a heuristic robustness interval by modifying the AGM interval semantics. For atomic predicates, it uses unnormalized predicate values for finer discrimination. For temporal operators, it incorporates a look-ahead evaluation and defines discounted child intervals. The heuristic information is used for search guidance, while the original interval semantics are retained for pruning and acceptance to preserve correctness. Frontier nodes are prioritized using a score based on heuristic robustness, time step, and accumulated path length. Dominance-based pruning is also applied, where only the top-K candidates are retained for nodes sharing the same graph node and time step. This pruning strategy, while potentially sacrificing completeness, significantly reduces the search space and is effective in practice when combined with heuristic prioritization. The document also outlines an experimental setup for evaluating a framework called GraSP-STL. This setup involves a 2D maze environment with an 8-DoF quadruped robot, an offline dataset of trajectories, and a diverse set of STL specifications generated from 12 templates categorized by difficulty (Basic, Intermediate, Advanced). These templates cover various temporal reasoning challenges, including reachability, sequencing, branching, persistence, safety constraints, and recurrent visitation objectives. The predicate evaluation function and its normalized version are also defined. The templates are designed to systematically increase in complexity, with advanced templates involving nested or multiple global operators requiring long-horizon reasoning. nodes.title: Results
nodes.summary:
The provided document excerpt details a graph-based framework called GraSP-STL for planning and executing tasks specified by Signal Temporal Logic (STL). It covers the experimental setup, including an environment and a reachability graph, and then delves into a specific STL specification with overlapping time windows and persistence constraints, highlighting the challenges these pose for planning. The document illustrates the planning process through statistics on node expansion and pruning, emphasizing the effectiveness of dominance pruning. It also presents the planned trajectory and its execution, showing close alignment. A robustness analysis demonstrates how predicate satisfaction and overall robustness evolve over time, consistent with interval semantics.

Furthermore, the excerpt describes a large-scale evaluation of the framework across 2400 tasks generated from 12 templates. Performance metrics like Planning Success Rate (PSR), Execution Success Rate (ESR), and Planning Time (PT) are reported, showcasing high success rates (95.58% PSR, 81.58% ESR) and scalability, even for long-horizon tasks. The analysis identifies strengths in handling temporal complexity and branching, but also limitations in sequential tasks with tight constraints and persistence tasks with consecutive global constraints, where execution slack is reduced. The conclusion summarizes the framework's contributions, its zero-shot capability, and outlines future work on slack-aware planning and adaptive graph refinement.
